Lesson 4. Stigma, prevention and help

1 · Lesson

Stigma is one of the biggest obstacles in mental health: it leads people to hide what is happening to them, delay seeking help and suffer discrimination. It includes stereotypes (such as the false idea that people with a mental disorder are dangerous), prejudice and self-stigma, when the person internalises those ideas.

Language matters: it is better to say "a person with schizophrenia" than "a schizophrenic", and to avoid using diagnoses as insults or metaphors ("the weather is so bipolar"). Direct contact with people who share their experience is one of the most effective ways to reduce stigma.

Prevention includes looking after sleep, physical activity and relationships, reducing alcohol and other drug use, and seeking help early. Knowing how to recognise warning signs in oneself and others (withdrawal, sudden changes, talking about not wanting to live) and knowing the resources (family doctor, in Spain the 024 line and 112) can make a difference.

2 · Example

If a friend tells you they are having a very hard time, you do not need to have the answer. It helps to listen without judging, ask directly whether they have thought about harming themselves (asking does not increase the risk), help them seek support and not carry that worry alone.

3 · Activity

For a week, notice how mental health is talked about around you, in series or on social media. Note stigmatising expressions and think how they could be said differently.
